title: Packet capture
summary: Read the wire with tcpdump: layers, ports, and the TCP handshake flags.

steps.title: Layers in one packet
body: A web request is a stack of envelopes, and a capture shows every one:
| Layer | What it says | Example |
| Ethernet | which hardware (MAC) on this wire | `02:42:0a:0d:01:0a` |
| IP | which host, end to end | `10.13.1.10 > 10.13.2.10` |
| TCP | which program (port), and connection state | port `8443`, flags `[S]` |
| HTTP | what the program asked for | `GET /reports/status` |
A tcpdump line prints IP and TCP; addresses end with `.port`:
```text
The server listens on a fixed port (`8443`); the client uses a random high one (`51234`).

steps.prompt: In this captured line, which port is the server's? Type the number.
steps.explain: The address after the last dot is the port. The client picks a random high port (51234); the server listens on a fixed one (8443).

steps.title: Handshake flags
body: ```text
client  -- [S]  SYN     -->  server    "I'd like to talk"
client  <-- [S.] SYN-ACK --  server    "OK, and I'd like to talk too"
client  -- [.]  ACK     -->  server    "Great"
tcpdump flag letters: `S` SYN, `.` ACK, `P` push (data), `F` FIN (close), `R` RST (reset/refused). A port scanner works by reading exactly these replies.
```text
tcpdump -ni any                    # everything, no name lookups
tcpdump -ni any host 10.13.2.10    # one host
tcpdump -ni any -A port 80         # one port, print payloads as text
tcpdump -ni any -c 20 -w out.pcap  # save 20 packets; read with -nr out.pcap
Filters combine with `and`, `or`, `not`: `tcp and src host 10.13.2.10`.
> **Try it for real:** the live lab *Packet capture: reading the wire* on the Labs page (needs Docker).

steps.prompt: Match each tcpdump flag field to its meaning.
Complete the command: capture on every interface, without name lookups, only port 80, printing payloads as text.
steps.explain: `-ni any` is `-n -i any`; `-A` prints ASCII payload.

steps.prompt: A capture shows `[S]` from the client to port 5432, then immediately `[R.]` back. What do you conclude?
options: The host is up but nothing listens on 5432
steps.explain: A reset is an active answer: the host's kernel saying no. A firewall drop would show `[S]` repeated with no reply.

steps.prompt: A reporting client talks plain HTTP (`GET /reports/status`) to its server through a shared router. What can anyone capturing on the path read, and what would TLS hide?
steps.explain: That's the whole reason TLS exists. Unencrypted protocols carrying sensitive data are a finding in any review.

steps.title: Parse a tcpdump line
prompt: Write `(string SrcIp, int SrcPort, string DstIp, int DstPort, string Flags) ParseLine(string line)` for lines like
The port is after the **last** dot of each address; the destination ends with `:`. `Flags` is the text inside the brackets (`S`, `S.`, `R.`).
starter: (string SrcIp, int SrcPort, string DstIp, int DstPort, string Flags) ParseLine(string line)
solution: (string SrcIp, int SrcPort, string DstIp, int DstPort, string Flags) ParseLine(string line)
hints: Split on spaces: word 2 is the source, word 4 the destination (strip the `:`).

steps.title: Read the handshake
prompt: Given the flags of a connection's packets in order, each prefixed with who sent it (`"c:S"`, `"s:S."`, `"c:."`), write `string Outcome(List<string> packets)`:
Look only at the packets up to the decision: extra data packets after an established handshake don't change the answer.
hints: Then look at the next packet (and the one after for the ACK).
